extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of rhetoric/classics; writers studying prose style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing classical rhetorical prose: how to construct members, phrases, and periods and how to choose among elevated, elegant, plain, and forcible styles, with their proper uses and vices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Members (cola): definition and function
rubrics_metrics.description: Members (cola) are the limbs/segments of prose which give rest and mark boundaries of discourse; a member must comprise a thought — either complete or a complete part of a larger thought — and indicate the conclusion of that thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members give the hearer a sense of completion; sometimes a member coincides with a complete thought, sometimes with an integral part. Treat members like the stones of a vault: they should support the structure of the period. Examples: short clauses like 'Darius and Parysatis had sons' function as complete members within a larger period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate length of members
rubrics_metrics.description: Members should not be made very long or excessively brief; both extremes are faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very long members make composition unwieldy and hard to follow; very short members produce the 'arid' composition. Use long members for elevated or stately passages; use short members for forceful, laconic, or small-subject passages. Exceptions allowed when matched to subject and tone (e.g., heroic subjects can have longer measures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrases (less than a member) and the virtue of brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'phrase' is that which is less than a member (a short clause or chip). Brevity is appropriate for apophthegms and maxims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compressing much thought into little space is a mark of skill; expanding a maxim into a long discourse turns it into rhetoric rather than a maxim. Use phrases for epigrams, sayings, and to increase force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period: definition and nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A period is a combined arrangement of members and phrases forming a portion of speech with a beginning and an end (a rounded, circular sentence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing the arrangement may preserve the subject matter but destroy the period. Periods should be dexterously arranged to fit the thought; their circular or rounded form creates the rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction rules for composite periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite periods are formed from multiple members; in composite periods the final member should be longer and statelier than the preceding ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The last member should as it were 'contain and embrace' the rest; a long, stately concluding member makes the whole period stately and impressive. If the concluding member is weak, the period limps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed number of members in a period
rubrics_metrics.description: Periods may consist of one to four members; anything beyond four transgresses due bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple periods can be single-membered when the member is sufficiently long and rounded. Smaller periods commonly have two members; the largest should be four.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of period and their characteristics (narrative, dialogue, oratory)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three kinds of period: narrative, dialogue, and oratory, each with particular formal qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative periods: neither overly moulded nor too relaxed—draw power from simplicity. Oratorical periods: tense, circular, neatly rounded and expectant (principle of suspense). Dialogue periods: lax, simpler, midway between resolved and compacted style; members may be flung together resembling the disjointed style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic vs disjointed style
rubrics_metrics.description: Two overarching styles exist: the compacted (periodic) style, consisting of periods, and the disjointed style, where members are not closely united.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extremes: neither a continuous string of accumulated periods (which becomes artificial and wearisome) nor a wholly disjointed method. Combine the two to be 'elaborate and simple'—neither untutored nor too artificial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of suspense and cadence in oratorical period
rubrics_metrics.description: Oratorical periods should contain tension and a rounded cadence that leads the hearer toward a definite goal; a period should create suspense and a concentrated ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The orator must shape rhythm and timing to maintain anticipation for the period's end; anticipate and forestall predictable endings at the speaker's peril.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four types of style: plain, elevated, elegant, forcible
rubrics_metrics.description: Styles fall into four main types: the plain (icyvds), the elevated (veyaXorperys), the elegant (yAadupés), and the forcible (Sevvds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each type has distinct subject-matter, diction, and compositional features and correlating vices; choose the style appropriate to speaker, subject, and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevated style (character and subdivisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The elevated style (characterized as the acme of stateliness) involves elevation in composition, subject-matter, and diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subdivisions: (1) elevation in composition/arrangement, (2) elevation in subject matter (noble themes), (3) elevation in diction. Beware frigidity—the correlative vice—arising at composition, diction, and subject, and culminating in hyperbole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frigidity as correlative vice of the elevated style
rubrics_metrics.description: Frigidity is the corrupt counterpart of elevation and may arise in composition, subject matter, or diction; its height is hyperbole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive loftiness that becomes cold or overblown; watch for instances where elevation tips into affectation or empty grandiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegant style (character and subdivisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The elegant style emphasizes charm and gaiety, with elegance arising in diction and composition and through sources in subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subdivisions: (a) kinds of grace and their elements; (b) sources of grace (figures, diction, composition); (c) sources in subject matter (proverbs, fables, comparisons, hyperboles); (d) elegant diction and composition; (e) beware the affected style (the correlative vice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain style (character and subdivisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plain style centers on plain subject-matter, plain diction, and plain composition, suited to clarity and directness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subdivisions: (1) plain subject matter, (2) plain diction, (3) plain composition. The arid style is its correlative vice; the epistolary style is regarded as a blend of plain and graceful styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forcible style (character and subdivisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The forcible style is characterized by forcible subject matter, composition, and diction aimed at intensity and vehemence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subdivisions: (1) forcible subject matter, (2) forcible composition, (3) forcible diction. Beware the unpleasant style, its correlative vice. Use brevity and tightened members to amplify force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of brevity to increase force
rubrics_metrics.description: Brevit y and concision amplify force and intensity; concise command or rebuke is more powerful than extended statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Laconic speech and compressed apophthegms (e.g., 'Dionysius at Corinth') are more forcible than detailed expostulation. For intense emotion or imperative statements favor short, concentrated members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple period (single-member period) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple (single-member) period requires that the sole member be of sufficient length and be rounded at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a single member lacks length or rounding, it does not function as a period. Examples: 'Herodotus of Halicarnassus sets forth...' and 'Clear expression floods with light the hearer's mind.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Antithesis and contrasted members
rubrics_metrics.description: Periods can be formed of contrasted or antithetical members; antithesis may be in thought or both thought and expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use antithesis to create parallel correspondences (article to article, connective to connective) and sustained symmetry. Examples include contrasted life paths or attributes (e.g., 'to the man he gave a life laborious and perilous, for the woman he made her beauty to be admired and coveted').

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetrical members and members with similar terminations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of symmetrical members and members with similar endings is a device, but requires caution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symmetry (like-with-like correspondence) and similar terminations can enhance balance and rhythm, but apply cautiously to avoid monotony or artificiality; the text contains specific cautions about their use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enthymeme vs period (distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The enthymeme is discussed as distinct from the period; they are different rhetorical constructs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand how an enthymeme (a rhetorical syllogism) differs from a period (a rhythmic, structural unit of prose); do not conflate logical argument structure with syntactic-periodic arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures of speech and special topics to employ judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Special topics to be considered include figures of speech, hiatus, metaphor, simile and comparison, onomatopoeic/ coined words, allegory, brevity/aposiopesis, epiphoneme, and poetical colour in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are enumerated as devices and areas for further instruction (see corresponding sections). Employ such devices to support the chosen style (elegant, elevated, plain, or forcible) and avoid their correlating vices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between variety and uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Good prose avoids excessive sameness—variety in members, rhythm, and periodation is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on one measure or pattern; avoid strings of identical periods (which tire the audience) and avoid monotonous aphoristic brevity; aim for appropriate variety to match subject and effect.
